**Finding submitted: `missing` (high severity), confidence 0.90**

**What I found.** Section 9 contains only cause-based exits — material breach (9.1), insolvency (9.2), and security/SLA/law/IP failures (9.3) — with 9.4 absent from the outline entirely. A document-wide search for "convenience" returned only the Order Form definition, confirming no convenience right exists for either party. Aggravating context:

- **§ 8.1** — three-year term (well beyond the 12-month threshold in the detection guidance).
- **§ 2.1** — USD 2,000,000/year take-or-pay commitment "without reduction or termination rights," which would defeat any convenience right even if one were added elsewhere.

That combination is the playbook's walk-away scenario: no Customer exit in a multi-year commitment.

**Redline (validated `ok:true`).** Two minimal operations:

1. New **§ 9.4** inserted after 9.3 — Customer convenience termination on 30 days' notice, in whole or in part, pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees, no early-termination fee or accelerated Fees, and no reciprocal Vendor convenience right during the term.
2. **§ 2.1** — replaced "without reduction or termination rights" with a carve-out subjecting the take-or-pay to Customer's termination and refund rights, including new § 9.4.

I left the take-or-pay volume commitment itself untouched to keep the edit proportionate, and drafted § 9.4 to align with the `seed-t4c` precedent language. The comment flags the fallback (60–90 days' notice with a fee capped at three months' Fees) as a negotiation path.

One item worth your judgment before this goes out: the § 2.1 carve-out is legally necessary for § 9.4 to function, but it does materially change the commercial bargain — a 30-day exit effectively converts a $6M committed spend into a month-to-month arrangement. Vendor will likely resist § 2.1 harder than § 9.4, and may argue the pricing was predicated on the committed volume. If the take-or-pay was priced concessions we wanted, the fallback (or a convenience right limited to Order Forms above the committed minimum) may be the more realistic landing zone.
